issues.description: The Methods state that all studies collected the CREP minimum of 120 participants, claimed to ensure adequate power. However, Table 1 reports sample sizes of 90, 90, 80, 116, 94, and 81 for six of the seven replications — all below 120. This directly contradicts the stated inclusion criterion and undermines the power justification, raising questions about whether inclusion rules were actually applied and whether the studies were adequately powered.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

issues.description: For the 'connect' outcome, the Results report a non-significant pooled effect (p = .065, 95% CI [-.01, .18] includes zero), but the Discussion states the meta-analytic effect was significantly different from zero. These are mutually contradictory; a p of .065 with a CI containing zero is not significant. This error directly affects the central conclusion about the connection variable.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.description: The fail-safe N for the 'express' outcome is reported as 3 in the Results but described as 5 in the Discussion. Such inconsistencies suggest reporting/computation errors and undermine confidence in the reported analyses.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant

issues.description: The fail-safe N for the 'connect' outcome is reported as 5 in the Results but as 11 in the Discussion. Beyond being internally inconsistent, this discrepancy compounds confusion about an outcome whose significance is itself reported inconsistently.
issues.quote: These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.description: The original study's effect size for 'advantageous self-disclosure' is reported as -.30 in the abstract and Results but as -.33 in Table 3 and the Discussion. The original comparator value should be fixed; this inconsistency affects effect-size difference computations and interpretation.
issues.quote: with widely varying and smaller effect sizes than the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.33)

issues.description: The fail-safe N (file-drawer) statistic is designed to assess the robustness of a significant meta-analytic result to unpublished null studies. It is misapplied here: (a) it is computed for the 'connect' outcome which was non-significant, where FSN is not meaningful; and (b) it is interpreted as evidence about whether future replications will find an effect or a 'lack of an effect,' which FSN cannot indicate. Pre-registered replications are also less subject to the publication bias FSN addresses.
issues.quote: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: interpretation contradicts data (null vs significant effect)
issues.description: The pooled effect for 'express' was statistically significant and positive (r = .08, p = .021, 95% CI [.01, .14] excluding zero), yet the abstract and discussion describe this as confirming that self-esteem 'did not relate' to self-expression. A significant pooled effect is being characterized as a null. The reliance on individual-study CIs including zero while ignoring the significant aggregate contradicts the logic of meta-analysis.
issues.quote: self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero)

issues.description: The prediction interval for 'express' is [.01, .14], which excludes zero, implying future studies are expected to show a (small) non-null positive effect. The authors nonetheless conclude a 'lack of an effect.' A PI excluding zero is inconsistent with concluding the effect is absent.
issues.quote: the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size smaller than the original study’s, all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study. The PI came close to, but did not include, zero so it may be that there is an effect

issues.description: The authors repeatedly infer publication bias in the single original study from the fact that replication effect sizes were smaller. A smaller effect in replications can arise from regression to the mean, sampling error in a small original (N=80), decline effects, or contextual moderators. A single original study cannot establish publication bias, and no formal bias test was applied.
issues.quote: the latter finding consistent with original study’s larger susceptibility to publication bias than replication studies

issues.subcategory: absence of power analysis / equivalence testing for null claims
issues.description: The authors conclude null relationships (e.g., for self-expression) and assert adequate power, but no a priori power analysis is presented, and no equivalence test (e.g., TOST) is conducted. Concluding the absence of an effect requires equivalence-based methods; the authors even acknowledge goals 2/6 (inferring/establishing equivalence to null) were 'not applicable,' yet then draw null conclusions.
issues.quote: We did not develop these studies expecting a null finding, so goals (2) and (6) are not presently applicable.

issues.subcategory: unreliable heterogeneity estimation with few studies
issues.description: Heterogeneity statistics (Q, T², I²) and their wide CIs (e.g., I² = 71.76%, 95% CI [27%, 95%] for safety; I² = 0%, CI [0%, 79%]) are estimated from only seven studies, where such estimates and between-study variance (tau²) are highly unstable. Although the authors acknowledge this, they still interpret heterogeneity (e.g., 'some evidence of heterogeneity') and rely on prediction intervals derived from these unstable estimates.
issues.quote: The between-study variance showed some evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 18.69, p = 0.005; T2 = .02, 95% CI [0, .15]; I2 = 71.76%, 95% CI [27.06%, 94.69%].

issues.description: The meta-analysis appears to pool correlation coefficients (r) directly via the 'rma' function with r and N, but it is not stated whether Fisher's z transformation was applied. Pooling untransformed r values can bias variance estimates and CIs, especially with larger correlations (e.g., safety values up to -.45). Methodological transparency on this point is needed for replicability.
issues.quote: The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters

issues.description: The prediction interval for 'connect' is reported as [-.09, .26] in the Results but as [-.07, .27] in the Discussion. This inconsistency in a key inferential statistic reduces confidence in reported numbers.
issues.quote: supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero

issues.description: The project acronym is expanded inconsistently: 'Collaborative Replication and Education Project' in the abstract versus 'Collaborative Research and Education Project' in the introduction. Though minor, this affects clarity and citation accuracy.
issues.quote: as part of the Collaborative Research and Education Project (CREP; Grahe, et al., 2016

issues.description: The replications were conducted 2016–2017, while the original was 2012, during which Facebook use among young adults declined and shifted to Instagram/Snapchat. The authors raise this as a possible explanation post hoc, but the changed social-media context threatens the comparability of replication and original, which is a fundamental interpretive limitation rather than a peripheral speculation.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others, whereas these platforms would not have been a consideration for participants in Forest and Wood’s (2012) study.

issues.description: One replication (SAU) ran participants in groups of two to six during data collection. Group administration of measures about self-disclosure and self-esteem may introduce non-independence and social-presence effects, differing from the other sites and from the original, yet this is not modeled or controlled.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.description: The key predictor (Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale) was administered with differing response scales (4-point vs 5-point) and altered item wording/order in some studies. Pooling these without examining measurement invariance or rescaling could affect the comparability of the self-esteem construct across sites, although effect-size r is somewhat robust to linear rescaling.
issues.quote: (b) most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale

issues.description: The authors acknowledge that scoring procedures differed (some studies averaged items, the Gordon study apparently summed them) and that analysis scripts, missing-data handling, exclusions, and item-level data were inconsistently documented or unavailable. This compromises full replicability and verification of the extracted effect sizes.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: Of 17 'forks' (teams that began the replication), only 7 are included, based on meeting minimum sample size and posting data/results. The fate and characteristics of the 10 excluded efforts are not described. Selective inclusion based on completion could introduce bias if non-completion related to results or sample characteristics.
issues.quote: These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository. All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis.

issues.description: Four separate outcome variables are tested across seven studies plus meta-analytic tests and effect-size difference CIs, with no adjustment for multiple comparisons. This inflates the family-wise error rate and is relevant given that several conclusions hinge on marginal significance.
issues.quote: we chose to calculate effect size r for all four outcome variables in the study

issues.subcategory: post hoc dismissal of original finding
issues.description: The original 'connect' finding (p = .05) is discounted using arguments about the relative likelihood of p-values near .05 under the null. While referencing the literature, this is a selective, post hoc rationale applied only to the outcome the replications failed to support, which risks confirmation bias in interpretation.
issues.quote: It is worth noting that the original study obtained a p-value of .05, and p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.description: Replication samples included substantially different age distributions from the original (means up to 26.2, SD up to 9.7, vs 21.35), indicating some sites recruited non-traditional students. Combined with gender-ratio differences, this affects comparability to the original undergraduate sample and the interpretability of pooled effects.
issues.quote: The average age in the seven datasets ranged from 19.3 to 26.2 (SDs ranging from 1.4 to 9.7), compared with 21.35 years for the original study.

issues.description: The manuscript makes strong self-promotional claims about novelty and 'cutting-edge' methods and emphasizes citation metrics of the original study as justification. These claims are not central to validity but overstate the contribution and substitute citation counts for substantive rationale.
issues.quote: Moreover, the novelty of the statistical methods used to assess the replicability of Forest and Wood (2012) made the present research an instrumental contribution to replication science.

issues.description: Effect-size difference tests compare each replication to a single, small original study (N=80) with wide CIs, making most differences statistically indistinguishable and limiting the informativeness of Goal-5 inconsistency analyses. While acknowledged, conclusions about consistency/inconsistency rest heavily on these underpowered comparisons.
issues.quote: This is primarily caused by the small sample size of the original study, as well as the rather small sample sizes of the replication studies.
